The second main misconception here, if I might just continue for one second, is that this would implicate all sorts of other types of data in which the Court has found more of a reasonable expectation of privacy, like email. Location history is different. I'm sorry, Justice Thomas.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Mr. Feigin, would you address Justice Alito's point as to this being an advisory opinion?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Frankly, Your Honor, we attempted to warn the Court about that in our brief in opposition. If the Court wishes to dismiss the case as improvidently granted, we're -- we'd be fine with that. I -- I do think there's really no chance the opinion here would make the officer's actions here unreasonable. Petitioner is suggesting now some kind of new kind of warrant requirement exception to the good-faith exception. I don't really understand how that would work or what the contours of it would be, and I don't -- like, what does it mean to have a new kind of warrant? At bottom, we just don't think there's anything that's going to happen here other than an affirmance. You would essentially have something that looks like an advisory opinion. I mean, I suppose the Court could say that the theoretical chance that something might happen is enough to keep this case alive, but I don't think that makes a great deal of sense.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: But in --

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Additionally, the policy, Google's policy, has changed. And would you compare that policy to this and the effect of that change?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Do you mean the pushing out of location history --

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Yes.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- so it's now stored on the phones?

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Exactly.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Well, I don't know that it would make a Fourth Amendment difference if Google were still able to comply with these warrants, but Google has represented to us that as of 2023 and that change that it made, it is no longer able to comply with the warrants, and that makes the difference.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: You --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: But other -- I'm sorry, Your Honor.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Go ahead.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: But, otherwise, if this were information that were exposed to Google, what Google -- I think it's an important feature of the warrant here that Google is actually the one doing the filtering on Google's accounts. As to any account except for the 19 that were additionally returned -- and, of course, they were all anonymized and they were truly anonymized -- their expert, if you look at page 288 of the court of appeals joint appendix, admits he wasn't able to specifically identify even the three people he was talking about. But, as to everyone else other than the 19, they might as well not have existed from the government's perspective.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Counsel --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: And even Google didn't really learn very much about them other than that they were not within this 150-meter radius circle during that particular hour. I question whether that is a -- an invasion of their reasonable privacy expectations. I think clearly not under this Court's decision in Knotts. That's a public place. These were public movements.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Counsel, if I could interrupt.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Sorry.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: One of the -- one of the central concerns that's been voiced, of course, is what's to prevent the government from using this to find out the identities of everybody at a particular church, a particular political organization. What are the restraints that would prevent that from becoming a problem?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Well, number one, Your Honor, would be the Stored Communications Act. And I respectfully disagree with Petitioner's counsel -- I mean, we have a somewhat different reading of the Stored Communications Act and exactly what it would require under these circumstances. And I know it's a statutory protection. But I disagree with counsel that it sets some kind of Fourth Amendment floor. The Court basically rejected that position in City of Ontario against Quon, which also involved the Stored Communications Act.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Well, put the statute --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Okay.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: -- to one side. Just in terms of the Constitution.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Putting the statute to the side, I mean, first of all, I don't think that there's any kind of categorical protection around something like a church. I mean, unfortunately, as you saw with Dylann Roof, we can have a shooting at a church. If he'd gotten away, we -- I would have thought this would be a law enforcement technique that might be useful.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: So you don't think there's any constitutional protection from such organizations to be subject to focused surveillance that would cover everybody in a particular location?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Well, I think one avenue that the Court has potentially held open, number one, is the amount of time for which the government could look. I don't know that the government could see everyone who came into a church at any time. I certainly --

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Well, if -- if services start at noon, they can go from noon to 1, however long they take.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: So let me make a few points on that, Your Honor. First of all, if someone doesn't want it known that they're going to a particular place, like a -- an abortion clinic, for example, they don't have to enable location history or keep it on while they are visiting that location. I mean, if there were a surveillance camera across -- at a bodega across the street from the church that could also see everybody who came in, then I don't think there'd be a claim to Fourth Amendment protection from government review of that. The second thing that I think I would say is that this has been -- the degree to which some -- someone can really be located in a particular location, I think, is somewhat overstated in this case. If you want to look at the sealed volume of the Joint Appendix, Joint Appendix Volume 3, you'll see that usually there's a fairly wide confidence interval of close to, you know, like, 30, 40 meters for everyone. So -- and that's only -- that only describes a circle with a 68 percent probability of containing them. So it's --

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Well, but I don't mean to --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- difficult to know exactly where they are.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: I mean, we don't -- we can't rely entirely on -- on good faith, but the point is not that they're looking for a particular individual, but they want to have a catalog of the people who go to a particular location. And it seems to me that that's a realistic problem.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Well, Your Honor, first of all, I mean, that can't -- that can't really happen under the Stored Communications Act.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Well, again --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: And the second --

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: -- put the statute to one side and just focus on the Constitution.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Okay. And the second thing I'd say is, you know, I would focus on this particular case, and in every case in which this has come up, the government has gotten a warrant because Google -- it's just easier to get Google to comply if we do get a warrant. And if you -- but, if you want to put the warrant aside, Your Honor, I do think that what really matters here is that people have affirmatively opted in. Only one-third of active Google account holders do that --

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: So, to prevent surveillance of sensitive locations, you have to rely on the fact that people are going to turn off something that many if not most people find is an important service?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Well, Your Honor, I do think, if you wish to conceal that you were at a particular location and you are effectively shouting and broadcasting your location to Google and that Google is creating, maintaining, using for any number of its own purposes those records -- I mean, Google could send you an ad saying --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Mr. Feigin --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- hey, I see you go to --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Mr. Feigin --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I'm sorry.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: -- I'm sorry to interrupt, but I -- I -- I -- I've got to think the answer to the Chief Justice's question is yes. This isn't a search. You don't think it's a Fourth Amendment search at all. You don't need a warrant. And, yes, if we want to determine everybody who is at a church or a political rally or the abortion clinic or anything else like that, we're -- we can do that as long as we can get Google to comply. Oh, and we might have a few tools besides warrants to get social media companies to comply with governmental requests.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: So I do think that effectively is our answer, Justice Gorsuch.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Yeah. Okay.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: We're not walking away from that completely.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Now -- now -- now --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I'm simply noting two --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Yeah. No, I -- no, I -- I understand that --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- very important features that -- of why.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: -- but that has to be your answer. And then -- and then there's a little tension in your argument as well. You're saying the sky will fall if you can't do this. You started off with that. That was the very first point you made, how important this is. And then, in the next breath, you said that Google can no longer provide this information because it has reconstructed how it operates. Can both things be true?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Yes, Your Honor, and here's why: I think a lot of the arguments that are being made here today and are made in the briefs, if accepted -- and I think, again, this is something Justice Jackson was getting at -- would have a debilitating effect on a number of other law enforcement techniques.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Like looking at email?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: So email, Your Honor, we get a warrant for email absent some --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: But -- but, again, you don't think you need one because they broadcast it, as you say, to Google. It's subject to very similar terms of service.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: That's not correct, Your Honor.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: No?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: We view email differently, and there are several reasons for that.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: How about Google documents? How about photos?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: We view all of those differently, and there are --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: So it's just location data that's different?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Yes.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Okay.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: And this Court has made clear that it's different. So, in Knotts, the Court makes clear that --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Could you just footnote that answer? Are they different because you treat them differently, or are they different because something in your theory -- theory doesn't apply to them?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Your Honor, if -- I was just getting to that. So we think they're different because the Court has always treated, like, the contents of one's personal thoughts as recorded differently from one's exposed public location, which is all that's at issue here at least for --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: How about a calendar?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: So your calendar I also think would be different from your location history because a record -- your own personal updated calendar of where you've been, and there are several reasons for that. I think the Court has made clear in Knotts that exposing your public location for two hours, you don't have a privacy expectation in that, and that contrasts sharply with cases like Ex Parte Jackson about physical letters or even a case like Katz, which is about telephonic --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: I interrupted Justice Gorsuch.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: No, no.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: And I --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- communications. Second, I think that's consistent with the original understanding of the Fourth Amendment. Justice Thomas gets into this a little bit in Footnote 8 at page 351 of his opinion in Carpenter about how the original focus of the Fourth Amendment was protecting personal confidences.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: He was -- he was a dissent there, though.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: On this particular point, Your Honor, I don't think there was -- it was inconsistent with --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Yeah, but, Mr. Feigin, I do think that Carpenter seems quite relevant to this, what you're now saying is location is different from email and photos and calendar appointments and everything else that people give to Google. And the reason is the location is just different because people just think that everybody knows where they are all the time. But I would have thought that Carpenter had something to say about that.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: So one point and then -- and then I have three different reasons why this case is different from Carpenter, but -- well, let me just jump to the three reasons because that's what you're asking about. Number one, we did exactly what Carpenter instructed us to do in this case. We got a warrant. Number two, I do think Carpenter and Jones --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: But you're saying you didn't need a warrant. So, I mean, I think the question is your theory, not what you did --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Okay. So --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: -- out of the goodness of your own heart.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- putting the warrant, which I think is the easy way to resolve this case, to one side, I think there are two key distinctions between this and Carpenter. One, in Carpenter, you had essentially the creation of CSLI, you know, Cell Site Location Information, as the price of even having a cell phone, which the Court had said in Riley was a device that basically nobody can live without. That's not the case here. You have people affirmatively --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Is that the -- the standard, the nobody-can-live-without-this standard?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: That's the one fixed point that the Court has given us, but, here, we're a long ways away from that because even one-third of active accounts -- of -- only one-third of active Google account holders bother to enable location history.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: So where -- where is the -- the -- the -- the line? If -- if 80 percent enabled this, would that -- would that make it a different case?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I think that would be much closer to Carpenter because I think, if I'm recalling correctly from Riley, it's something like 90 percent of people have cell phones. But I certainly think one-third of active Google account holders, which is a fairly small percentage of the world's population overall, shows that people don't need this. You can use Google Maps without location history. You can use Google Maps even without a Google account. The second thing I would say about Carpenter is that although neither Carpenter nor some of the separate opinions in Jones, like Justice Alito's opinion that you joined, drew clear temporal lines, I do think both Jones and Carpenter -- both the opinions in Jones and Carpenter focus on detecting the patterns of life and long enough periods of location to show the patterns of life. I don't think two hours is enough to show the patterns of one's life. They might show that you went to a church once. It doesn't show that you're a regular churchgoer. It might show that you went to a doctor's office. It doesn't show why.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: I guess one -- I guess one question would be why is it -- why -- why would the only thing that you would have an interest in protecting is the patterns of one life as opposed to the things that you do in one's life that you particularly don't want people to know about, such as going to a political event, going to an abortion clinic, et cetera? It's like you can -- I can tell you a lot of things about the patterns of my life. What I really want to keep private is particular things that I might do, you know, on very discrete occasions.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Well, two points, Your Honor. One is I think the fundamental insight of Knotts is that if you walk out in public and you walk into some sensitive location, then you are exposing all of that to public view. In Knotts, they were following people to private residences. They didn't follow them into the private residences, but they were following people to private residences through the use of a beeper and stopping outside the private residence. Maybe you don't want someone to know that you're having an affair, but if you have a beeper in your car under Knotts and they're following you for two hours, they will find that out. Number --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Would your position be the same if you had picked up Mr. Chatrie in his home?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: If -- well --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: If it had revealed his --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- there's testimony at page 120 of the Joint Appendix from this Court that shows that we couldn't locate which of the houses was his even though he eventually did go to a house because, as it turns out, because the confidence intervals were simply too --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: But -- but --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: But could you?

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: -- your -- your -- your position would remain the same regardless whether somebody was in his home at the time?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Well, Your Honor, I guess I would make a couple points. I think that -- I think that we would argue that. I think the Court could draw a distinction. And the reasons we would argue that it would still remain the same is, number one, we had no warrant. Number two, I think this would make this case somewhat like Karo, where it doesn't invalidate the law enforcement technique ab initio. It just means that someone with standing could suppress the information about the particular home. And, number three, I think this is distinct from other home circumstances precisely because of the opt-in and the fact that the person is advertising the fact that they are at home, sharing that with Google, and Google could say: You know, I see -- I mean, Google could say: I see you go to church every Sunday, maybe you'd be interested in this particular religious item. Google could say: I see you're often in the house on Saturday mornings, maybe you'd be interested in this particular thing that could be delivered to your house on Saturday mornings. And so they are opting to share that information to get a purely voluntary service. And they're doing so, if you want to look at the terms of service, which we don't -- which we agree aren't controlling, subject to the full knowledge that Google -- of what Google is doing with it, and the ability of Google to respond in good faith to law enforcement or to make any number of other choices like sharing with service providers for Google that will expose that information to public view.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Mr. Feigin, are you really saying -- I mean, you're leaning pretty heavily on the -- the -- the -- the correct proposition that what you do in public view is not generally -- you don't have a reasonable expectation of privacy in. But now you're telling Justice Kagan, really, that if you go into a private home, it wouldn't be a search? I mean, if you trace --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Well --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: -- trace location services? I mean, I understand in this case --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- just the --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: -- and is that true, that in this case, you're saying he didn't -- you didn't pick him up in any home?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Well, Your Honor, he was -- he -- he eventually stopped at the end of his journey away from the bank at a group of homes, but there's testimony, this is page 120 of the Joint Appendix --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: But not inside the home. You didn't --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: We couldn't tell which home he was even in.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Yes. Okay. But you really are saying that you could track someone going inside a home, Justice Sotomayor asked Mr. Unikowsky about movements inside a home, movements to the bathroom, movements to the bedroom, all of that, if the confidence interval is narrow enough?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Your Honor, I think -- I think what I'm saying is two things. One, I do think we could have done that here because of the warrant, like under Carroll.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Okay. But I think the question is, is that a search under your theory?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Is it a search? I -- I don't -- I think probably, Your Honor. Like, I acknowledge that's going to be a much harder case for us.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: But no is your answer?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I think if we were to argue that -- I think -- I'd like to reserve the possibility that we could argue that it's not a search principally because of the opt-in and the broadcasting, but, look, I fully accept that that would be a very, very difficult argument to sustain. Nothing in our argument in this case depends on it. And I -- I'm not, like, saying that that -- that that's critical to our argument. And if the Court thinks that that is a bridge too far, I'm fine with that.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Well --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I would just have it on the proposition.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: -- except for it's totally inconsistent with your theory, but other than that.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Other than that, Justice Gorsuch.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: On -- on the particularity side, Mr. Feigin, let's say you go to a hotel, and the -- the warrant is search all the rooms in the hotel for the gun on the bedside, or a storage facility, search all the storage units for a particular contraband, or to a bank, go search all the safe deposit boxes for the pearl necklace that's been stolen. What's the difference between those cases and this case, assuming that I have a term of service with the hotel, with the storage facility, with the bank that says you can access these places from time to time for purposes that we agree upon and, of course, you -- you can -- you can do something with the government, if -- IF the law allows it?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: So, Your Honor, I think this is a somewhat -- this goes to a somewhat under-theorized portion of the Fourth Amendment, which is the definition of a place. I think we often have an intuitive sense of what's a place. In particular, with an apartment building, I think --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: You -- you would agree those warrants would all be impermissible?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I don't know about -- necessarily about storage locker 1, that would probably be impermissible. Certainly, we couldn't search every apartment in a building, both because homes are first among equals and because --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Well, hotel -- hotel rooms, bank, safety deposit boxes, storage facilities, the warrants I've just described, go search for the contraband, the gun, the pearl necklace, okay or not okay? Are those sufficiently particularized?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Well, let me take them each in turn because I think the analysis might be slightly different under -- under each of those things, Your Honor. First of all, for the apartment homes, no. And I think that's --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Still haven't asked about -- about apartments. I asked about hotels, but --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I'm sorry. A hotel is the same because the Court has treated it as a home.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Okay.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: And houses are specifically listed in the Fourth Amendment --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: All right.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- and they're first among equals.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: How about the other two?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Okay. I think -- a storage locker, I think probably we could not do that, so -- and I think we probably couldn't do a storage room, although it would depend how it's organized. But if --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Like every storage facility in America, you know, with one of those awful rolling gates and a padlock at the bottom.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: So let me explain why and why that's different from this case, if I could.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: I'm just asking you, do you think that warrant would be sufficiently particularized, the one I described? Yes or no?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I think it would be sufficiently particularized because it would describe what the government had a basis to search for.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: The government --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- but what I don't --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: -- the government could ask the storage facility and require them to search every locker in 500 lockers for the contraband?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: What I don't think is that it describes a discrete Fourth Amendment place in which to search for the things that the government --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Okay. So it's not particularized, then?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: So I -- I think it's --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: I mean, it really --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- more about place than particularization there, assuming there's probable cause to believe that the area writ large is going to contain the contraband. If I could explain a little further on this, Your Honor. I think what makes the difference in some of these hypotheticals versus what we have here --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Well, first, I just want an answer to my hypotheticals, and then we'll get to here, if that's all right.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Your Honor -- Your Honor, my answer to the hotels is no. My answer to the other two is very likely not.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Okay.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Yeah, I would need to know a little more about it.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Okay. All right. And now--

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: And now let me explain why --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: And now turning to this, do you agree that -- that Google had to query every single user's account?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: No.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Well, you said so --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I mean, I -- I --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: -- on page 10 of your brief.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Do you mean query in the -- do you mean "query" as like a synonym for the First Amendment sense?

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: I'm using your words, from page 41.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Oh, okay. Yes, I do agree Google had to query in that sense. I'm sorry.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: And -- and there are

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I thought you meant "query" as a synonym for "search."

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: -- about 500 million users accounts, right?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Yes, I agree with that.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Okay. All right.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I agree, and let me tell you why it's different. I think the reasons the hypotheticals -- the -- I -- but I apologize for misunderstanding your use of "query" as a synonym for "search." The -- the reason this is different is I think it's a lot about opacity and control. And what I mean by "opacity" is the separateness of the different spaces. And control is who has control over those spaces. Here is a case where I think, as the Court recognized in Riley, can often happen. The physical analogies kind of break down to some degree. The Court has been clear in Smith against Maryland --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: But let's -- let's just stop there.

turns.name: FEIGN
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Let's -- let's assume that these accounts are -- are kept in what you can call opacity or whatever you want, but are kept in the same kind of discrete manner as your -- as your e-mail is.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Well, Your Honor, I don't think that's the case here. I think what's happening --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Let's assume it is. Let's assume it is. Let's assume that the Google user account -- we have -- we've got a lot of briefs on this.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: So, Your Honor --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: They're -- they're categorized similarly by user and -- and walled off from other users, both the e-mail and the location data. Let's assume they're similar in that respect.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Your Honor, if this were a record that the user created and uploaded, our answer to this case would be different, but if this is -- but in this case, this is a record that Google creates, Google software sends it, Google processes it, it runs its own algorithms to actually figure out what information it's storing. It is data that Google maintains and data that Google accesses for any number of reasons. If we were to have a physical analogy to storage lockers -- and I'm not sure how useful these physical analogies are -- it's like having a bunch of storage lockers where there's a glass wall in front of them instead of having an opaque door for each box. All the government is asking for here is to get in the room and look at the front of those storage lockers. I don't think that the limited amount that even Google sees at step 1 is going to be considered a search. And for -- as I said earlier, from the government's perspective, all of those other storage lockers, if you want to call them that, and we're accepting that analogy for purposes of this answer, all of those other storage lockers might as well not exist. For all the government knows, they -- there are only 19 people --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Is that because --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- who have --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Mr. Feigin, is that because, at step 1, unlike the examples that we've been talking about, you don't know how many apartments there are? You don't know how many storage lockers there are? At step 1, it's just like getting a list. There are 16 apartments in this building, right? Isn't that -- I mean, that's why I'm appreciating a difference between the steps as the iterative process with Google goes forward. Step 1 is we have a bank robbery. Here's the bank. We would like to know how many cell phone accounts were in this radius during this period of time? Right? I mean, you don't have the names. You don't have anything more than that. I'm -- I'm struggling to understand the step 1 problem, other than to figure out how the government came up with 150 meters and 30 minutes before and after. So can you start maybe by answering that question? Where -- where does that number -- where do those numbers come from?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Sorry. I can't help you're struggling with step 1 because I too don't see a problem with step 1. But the 150-meter radius and the half an hour before and half an hour after were based on wanting to exclude -- there's some testimony in the record about this. They did want to include the church because they had testimony about a suspicious car that had been parked at the church. And they thought the robber, as it turns out, directly might have come from there.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: So evidence was presented to the magistrate. The reason why we're making the circle this big to include these structures is because there could be some connection to this robbery?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I don't believe that evidence -- that particular reason for including that was presented to the magistrate --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Okay.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- no.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: All right.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I'll just explain to you how they got 150 meters. And half an hour before and half an hour after allows you some information about, for example, there was a reference -- and the magistrate did learn this -- to co-conspirators in the demand note. And you might want to see if someone dropped the robber off or someone picked up the robber afterwards. You want to know more about the movements around it. The advantage the magistrate has that I think is difficult for a reviewing court to replicate is knowledge of local conditions and realizing that 150 -- if I could just finish this sentence, Your Honor --

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Sure.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: 150 meters in Midlothian, Virginia isn't likely to turn up the entire phone book.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. Justice Thomas, anything further? Justice Alito?

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: You've been asked quite a few questions that analogize what happened here to searches, old-fashioned searches, of physical places, so searching the room of everybody in a hotel. If that happened, I think there'd be an awful lot of angry hotel guests, all of those who had nothing whatsoever to do with the crime. Here Mr. Unikowsky says 500 million people were injured when there was a search for their data, even though it was completely a anonymized. How many of those 500 million people have come forward to complain about anything like this, which may be going on every day?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Well, I think that's right, Your Honor. I think, that points out if they did want to complain, that would be a separate Fourth Amendment standing question, of course, and I -- I don't think that Petitioner here can represent their standing but one reason they wouldn't complain is, first of all, I don't think this would violate the reasonable expectations of privacy even if the government were doing it. Second of all, Google was doing it and it's no different from any number of other things that Google does for it's own -- for it's own particular purposes. But the --

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Would you think that -- don't you think that makes a difference for Fourth Amendment purposes, the distinction between a law enforcement officer invading a physical space and a request to a company to conduct a search with which the company complies?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Well, not only do I think that, Your Honor, but I think the Court has said that multiple times. If you look at cases like Oklahoma Press against Walling or Lone Steer. It's very different when a than officer comes into the premises and looks around versus something that functions, although this had the protections of the warrant, in many ways it functioned like a subpoena in that it was the provider doing the filtering and the provider disclosing the records, which limited what the government saw considerably. The only non-anonymized information the government got was for three individual users. It didn't know anything about anyone in the sensor vault, other than the 19 that were returned for step 1. And as to them, it didn't know their identities.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: You've heard --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I do think that's -- that's critical. But the argument that he's trying to make about step 1, I think it's very important that it really does implicate tower dumps, for example, because in -- it implicates any number of law enforcement techniques that might incidentally find data about someone else. Let's -- even a CSLI warrant, you might have a company that organizes its data by tower. And in order to find, let's call them Carpenter, in order to find Carpenter's CSLI data, the company has to search across all of its towers during the time period and figure out which ones are Carpenter and which ones aren't. It's going to learn everything about all its users in theory. I mean, I'm sure it's using software to do this and having a filtering mechanism, just like Google did here, but it's going to learn everything about all its users for that period of time. I don't know how he distinguished that. For tower dumps --

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Let's --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- I don't know how he distinguished --

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Tower dumps are not before us. E-mail are not before us. Calendars are not before us. Photos are not before us. I mean, I understand that if we're going to write a treatise on the application of the Fourth Amendment to the new digital world, we might want to include sections of all of these things, but none of those things is at issue in the actual case or controversy -- controversy that is before us. You've heard some proposals about narrow theories on which the case could be decided that would, as I understand them, focus on whether there was a lack of probable cause or a lack of particularity at step 2 or step 3. What would be the precedential importance of a decision like that which turns on the particular warrant that is at issue in this case?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Well, Your Honor, unless the Court upholds the warrant, I do think the Court needs to reach the search questions in some way because the Court would have to address whether the warrant was even necessary. And I think as I've tried to make clear the Court -- a lot of the arguments that Petitioner is making here, while those other techniques are not directly at issue, would have implications on a lot of those other techniques and would create a lot of litigation and have a potentially debilitating effect on law enforcement. But -- they could even affect such things as visual camera surveillance. But as to the specific question you asked about the particularity at steps 2 and 3, I do think it was sufficiently particularized because you had geospatial and temporal coordinates that showed these people might be either suspects or witnesses, and the government simply was able to obtain enough information to figure out which of them might have information or be worth identifying. And I -- I -- I think that the Court has been clear that those are permissible law enforcement interests. The Court might say that --

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Well, let me just --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I'm -- I'm sorry.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Let me just -- I -- I don't want to take up too much time. Let me just ask one final question. Of all of the arguments that Petitioner has raised, which do you think would be the most disruptive of what everybody has understood to be the limitations of the Fourth Amendment up to this point? His argument that this is a general warrant, his argument that he had a property interest in the -- in this data that was collected by Google? His request that we treat this search by a company as if law enforcement officers were themselves searching through records? Which of the -- which is the worst?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Is all of the above an option, Justice Alito?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I do think the idea that you have a privacy right or a property right in even a moment's worth of location history could be debilitating to all sorts of types of visual surveillance. The agent theory could debilitate subpoenas. The property theory, I don't even know where the Fourth Amendment goes after that. And I -- I -- I do think a lot of these theories are -- and the general warrant theory that Your Honor mentioned, I think, would call into question how we do a lot of computer warrants. We often name the servers as the place to be searched. And I -- I don't frankly know, and I don't think courts are well equipped to find out, exactly how data is organized within a particular company. And I don't know whether we have to take discovery on that in every case where we seek a warrant and actually really go down to the nuts and bolts or the virtual nuts and bolts of how a company does this.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: All right, thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Sotomayor?

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: A few questions. Number 1, the Stored Communications Act, a violation, Mr. Unikowsky said, may be a violation, there may be criminal penalties for it, but it doesn't give a suppression remedy, correct?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: That's right.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: All right. Number 2, you're saying everything would be horrible but Carpenter has already said you need a warrant, correct, for data?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: And we got a warrant here, yes.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: All right.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: And --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: But you're saying I didn't need a warrant because it was a short period of time. Assuming I disagree with that

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Well, Your Honor --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Just assume. Okay? There are three steps to this process. Were the three steps approved by the warrant? I read the warrant but now I've forgotten. Were the three steps approved?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Yeah, the three steps were all laid out within the warrant -- within the warrant itself.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: But the one who made the choice at step 2 and step 3 was the -- was Google, not a magistrate, correct?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Well, Your Honor, the warrant required the government to make reasonable efforts to minimize between steps 1 and 2 and step --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Well, usually isn't it -- I thought that if, for the foreign sovereign -- for the foreign checking system that we have, that magistrate judge says you have to minimize as you're doing it, but come back to us if you want a greater scope. Correct? And here you went from 30 minutes to two hours. And you didn't get a magistrate judge --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: That was expressly authorized within the warrant. The warrant's parameters said that step 2 would be an hour before and an hour after the robbery.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Okay. I thought it was two hours. Maybe I misunderstood.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: That's a total of two hours --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: I see. All right.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- Your Honor, one hour before and one hour after.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: I misunderstood that.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: The original was an hour -- a half hour before, a half hour after.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: There are, I understood, many jurisdictions in which the government is going back at step 2 and step 3, correct? That's not much of a burden.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: So --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: If you have gotten step 1 and you can explain you're reasons for why you're narrowing the warrant and -- and why you need it at step 2, you could do that.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: We -- we could do that and with more recent warrants, the government has done that. Obviously this was a Virginia warrant but just to defend this warrant for one second, I think the Court recognized in Scott, which was a case we cite in our brief, that -- which is under the Wire Tap Act, not directly a Fourth Amendment case but the same principle applies --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Now there's value, isn't there, in our saying something like or deciding we need a warrant, it has to be particular as to time, place, time, and it has to explain the reasons why those limitations are reasonable because that's always a part of a warrant search? And wouldn't that have value for the dispute that's going on around the country and between and among judges even on this Court? Some said there was -- some took your position that there's no right of privacy whatsoever and you don't need a warrant. Others have taken the position that you need a warrant, but you don't need much supervision from the magistrate judge. There is value in our setting the parameters of this process, isn't there?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I think, if the Court were to say something about warrants, that could have value. And I'm not going to claim that the sky is going to fall if we had needed a separate warrant at steps 2 and 3 and a total of three warrants. We've actually done that in more modern times. But what I am saying is that I would caution the Court against saying that it's -- that warrants can never include any kind of discretion like the warrant did here because --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: We don't need -- we don't need to say that.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: You --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: We -- we -- if all we said was you generally need particularity, the way you do in any situation, you have to give enough to say there's a reasonable probability or fair probability, I think, is our language, that evidence is in a particular -- would -- would be disclosed, and what -- it's a limited search to these times and places, and you have to do it at each stage of a warrant.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Your Honor, I think we met all of those requirements here.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: We don't even -- I don't even know if we need to go that far, but you would not be troubled by that rule?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Your Honor, you're simply describing what the Fourth Amendment requires. And as we've laid out --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: All right. That's exactly --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- in our brief --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: That's exactly --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- we think the Fourth Amendment satisfies those requirements -- our warrant -- I'm sorry -- our warrant satisfies those Fourth Amendment requirements.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: I'm not quite so sure of that because you don't explain why it's narrow, but that's a different issue.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Well, Your Honor --

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- if I could be --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: All right. Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Kagan?

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Mr. Feigin, I'm going to give you one of those physical location hypotheticals that you're going to resist, but you'll have a chance to tell me why it's different. But I -- I want to understand your theory, and the easiest way for me to do it is through these. So let's go back to what Justice Gorsuch said. Let's use the -- the storage locker. And there's a storage locker facility in town, it has 500 storage lockers, and they have a relationship with the police chief so that the police chief can come to them and ask the storage locker manager to search all the storage lockers for particular things that the police chief needs. So the police chief goes to the storage locker manager, and he says we're looking for somebody with a particular kind of weapon. You know, we're looking for somebody with a Glock. And -- and the manager goes through each of the 500 lockers, and he comes back to the police chief and he says: I've got a list for you. We have eight lockers with -- that contain a Glock. And now we're going to have a further conversation, you and me, the manager and the police chief, about which of these eight you really want, all right? And they do that. So, in that situation, how many of the lockers would you say have been searched and how should a warrant respond to that? In other words, have 500 lockers been searched? Has -- have eight lockers been searched? Or have zero lockers been searched?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I think some of that might depend on exactly the circumstances under which the proprietor of the storage facility was permitted to go into these storage lockers, because that might set some of the parameters of the reasonable expectation of privacy or at least inform them. I also think it's distinct from the circumstances we have here because you actually have someone who more plausibly could be seen to be acting as a government agent than the recipient of a warrant or a subpoena or an order of production from the court.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: No, what I'm -- I guess what I'm saying is just assume that the relationship is similar to the relationship between Google and the government, and just assume that the terms are similar to the terms that Google has with its customers. So all of that is the same.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: So there --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Five hundred lockers searched, eight lockers searched, zero lockers searched?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Your Honor, I think, to the extent we're talking about physical objects that are put into a storage locker that is expected to remain locked except when the user comes and wants to take something out of it, I think we might say the -- that that was a search of all of the lockers because someone went in and looked in every single locker.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: And so what would you need for a warrant for that search?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I think we'd need probable cause that there was going to be a Glock in one of the lockers, but I think -- I'm not -- I am --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: So you couldn't -- you couldn't get it for all 500?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- I am uncertain that would be valid for the reasons I was discussing with Justice Gorsuch in that those might all be separate Fourth Amendment places, and we'd need specific probable cause as to each. I don't think that's true of the database that Google maintains because --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Okay. So what is the difference in your view?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: So I think the difference in our view is, first of all, to the extent that I heard opposing counsel -- and this is in their brief -- just suggest that Google's database is quite large, I don't think that in and of itself is a problem. I mean, obviously, you could get a warrant to search a large house where the rooms are accessible to one another or a large file room even if it's physically separated across multiple rooms in a facility. I think the main difference here is that the -- and, you know, Your Honor, here, I maybe am going to resist the physical analogy a little bit, but I don't think that these are the same thing as discrete storage lockers. These are more like storage lockers that don't have the set of expectations that I was just positing in answer to your hypothetical and really are like a bunch of storage lockers with a glass wall. You could imagine, Your Honor, a coat check where we know that somebody dropped off drugs at the coat check and we know what the person's name is. We don't know the coat check number. On their view, we couldn't get a warrant to go look at all the bags for the ID on -- on the bag that -- for the ID matching the person who dropped off the bag because those would be unnatural bag searches that would be unlawful under the Fourth Amendment, and so we'd wind up searching everybody's bag. I think this is somewhat addressed somewhat obliquely, I suppose, by the citation we have on page 44 of our brief to Chapter 8 of Professor LaFave's treatise, which allows for, even in a bailment situation -- we don't think this is a bailment situation -- but even in a bailment situation, there's general agreement among courts that the bailee, the person with possession of the property, can look at it for -- on behalf of law enforcement within the terms of the bailment. And, here, what you have -- again, we deny that it's a bailment, but if you want to analogize this to some kind of bailment scenario like you might have with the storage lockers, we'd still be within the terms of the bailment because Google wasn't doing anything other than stuff that Google could already do.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Thank you, Mr. Feigin.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Gorsuch? Justice Kavanaugh?

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: You always get a warrant, you said, and the states always get a warrant. So, in terms of practical problems that would ensue, I gather there would be no practical problems -- I understand your legal theory, but no practical problems from our saying that a warrant is required. Is that accurate for these particular kinds of warrants?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Your Honor, if the Court were to say that this warrant was fine, we have no --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: That wasn't my question.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Ah. Well, I mean, Your Honor, I think it is a huge caveat --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: The question was, are there any practical problems that you want to identify with our --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: With getting a warrant in particular?

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Yes.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I don't --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: And I assume the answer's no because you've many times today said we always get a warrant in response to tests, so --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: That -- that's right, Your Honor, my answer is no, but I would worry about an -- an opinion that --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: How we say that, I get that.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: What you say.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Yes.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: But, like, I -- I do -- I don't think we've had practical problems getting the warrants we need in these cases.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: And then, if -- if a warrant's required, it comes down to how particular, I think, correct --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Yes. I -- I -- I do think --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: -- it has to be in describing -- and on that, I just want to -- I think you're going to agree with this, but I just want to get this out there, and you tell me. There's a big difference between the issuing judge and the reviewing judge. That's the good faith. And the issuing judge, it seems to me, we should set some parameters, reasonable -- temporal scope, reasonable geographic scope, but then we trust issuing magistrates around the country to implement those rules. When it comes to the reviewing judge, we don't micromanage in second-guessing what the issuing judge did so long as it doesn't exceed, you know, certain bounds that we've set forth. Is that correct?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Yes.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: And what should we say, if we say reasonable, temporal, and geographic bounds for these kinds of geofence warrants, is that all we need to say? Maybe we should -- you want us to say that one is in this case, should we get into the -- this case or should we just say it has to be reasonable, temporal and geographic bounds and -- and send it back to Justice Alito's first question? We're on a -- we're at the reviewing stage, not the issuing stage here.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Your Honor, I think that would probably be the better course because, you know, I think what this Court's centuries, frankly, of Fourth Amendment jurisprudence teaches is that it's difficult to put a ton of meat on the bone of reasonableness in this context or probable cause or reasonable suspicion or -- or any of these standards because they're --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: This is particular. How particular, you know, is 150 meters okay? 200 okay? It strikes me micromanaging that's going to be problematic and it's really problematic when you're distinguishing the issuing judge from the reviewing court down the road, given what we've said reviewing courts have to be extraordinarily deferential.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Yeah. And I think the Court could direct some attention to the magistrate about, you know, not wanting, as -- as I was suggesting to Justice Jackson, drawing parameters that under local conditions are likely to turn up much more than the government needs. But I would --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Exactly. Exactly. If we say things like that, that should -- we trust the -- issuing judges around the country do this every day to make --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: You -- you should trust them, Your Honor. And frankly our incentives are perfectly aligned with theirs. Because when we're seeking a warrant like this, we don't want more information than we really need because that just increases the noise-to-signal ratio and makes these more difficult to actually find the -- the criminals. I believe there are some suggestion from opposing counsel that -- that often these warrants get abandoned or -- or quashed and they don't really turn up much evidence of crime. And that may be because some law enforcement agencies -- I'm not impugning any specific one, we have many wonderful law enforcement partners -- aren't drawing the parameters narrowly enough to even help themselves. Everyone's incentives are aligned here.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Barrett?

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: So you describe Mr. Unikowsky's position as maximalist but there's a risk of the government's position being maximalist the other way. And I think, you know, two particular concerns are the ability to track into private residences and you didn't concede that. The other is calendar, photos, e-mail. Can you -- you -- you -- did -- did I understand you before to say that you are conceding that would be different and that would be a search?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Yes. And I -- I -- I do concede that tracking into a private residence without a warrant, I think, is a very, very difficult argument for us to make. And I'm not -- I'm frankly not sure that we would actually make it. I was simply noting that unlike in Karo where the Court held that we would have needed a warrant --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Sure.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- which was quite clear

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: But you didn't rule -- you didn't rule it out.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: I -- I understand that.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I -- I'm -- I didn't want to categorically rule it out.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Right. But you are saying that you would need a warrant for calendar, photos, e-mail?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Yes.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: That would be a search?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Yes. And let me -- I mean, I -- I'm happy to --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Sure. I mean, if you want to --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- explain again --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Well --

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: -- why -- why I think that would be.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: I -- I just wanted to make sure we had a crisp of understanding what the government's position was on that. So that's why I asked it.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Yes, that -- that's the government's position on both of those issues.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Jackson?

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Yes, really quickly. I -- I think there's something about the iterative process that may matter. And so just taking Justice Kagan's hypo really quickly for an understanding of what is happening, tell me if the government is thinking about it in this way. You keep saying this is like storage lockers with glass fronts, with pieces -- with glass on the front of it. They don't have solid doors, anyone can look and see what's in there. So step 1 is the government saying tell us if, by looking at these lockers, any include -- have bags in them that might have a gun in them. Give us the list of the ones or how many have that, I think is a sort of a step 1 concern. And then maybe step 2 is once you've gotten that subset, open the lockers, and, you know, see if there's really a bag or feel if there's really a bag and then, step 3 is open the bags inside each of the lockers. I feel like there's something happening with the way in which Google is providing this information in response to the government that may be requiring more probable cause or more particularity as you go along. So what is the government's thought about that?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Your Honor, with my continuing caveat that I think there's a limited utility in some of these physical analogies, I would kind of resist breaking it down exactly that way. I think step 1, you know, if we want to use the gun example, step 1 might be more, okay, you've got a glass partition here, tell us which of them have guns in them. Number 2 would be okay, of that subset, continuing to look through the glass wall, you don't need to open it for this because this is still stuff that is exposed to your view, please tell us which of them have a gun and a box of ammunition. And then step 3 is, okay, for the two or three you found, please tell us who's rented those storage lockers.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Do you agree that you need more to get to each step? I -- I mean, here what criteria did -- did the detectives use to narrow down the list from the 19 to the nine to the three that were ultimately there? And wouldn't a particularized warrant need to have some criteria in it to guide law enforcement at each of these stages?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: So Your Honor, with a -- with apologies, I think I need to take a step back and say that I don't really view this as getting more particularized. I believe there is enough probable cause to -- that the original warrant was -- and the 19 people that turned up, probable cause to believe those people would be either witnesses or suspects. And then there's a question of how to figure out which ones to follow up on. So what you actually have here is a warrant that I think is fully particularized with probable cause the whole way through.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: You could have gotten the 19 names from the beginning?

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: I think that we -- I think that we could have. But in order to maximize privacy, what happened here was that the warrant included a minimization requirement on the government at each step, which is akin to the kind of minimization requirement you see in the Wire Tap Act.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Okay, thank you.

turns.name: ERIC J. FEIGIN
turns.text: Okay. Thanks.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. Rebuttal, Mr. Unikowsky?

turns.name: ADAM G. UNIKOWSKY
turns.text: Thank you, Your Honor. So I'd like to say a few words about why this was a search, a few words about the warrant, and then finally why the Court should decide the case. First why this was a search. I welcome counsel's concession from the podium that if there was a search for something like -- something else in the cloud like e-mail or calendar entries or photographs, in that case there really would be a search and a warrant would be needed. But although I welcome that concession, I just don't understand the distinction that is drawn between those types of data and this type of data for Fourth Amendment purposes, either under a property or a privacy lens. So under a property lens, a person's relationship to their location information is the same thing as their relationship to their photographs or to their e-mail. It's in their password protected account. Counsel suggested that the answer might be different because it's in some way raw data, it's sort of generated by your phone as opposed to sort of a creative writing. So first of all, it's generated by the person in the sense that you move around. And second of all, I don't understand why that distinction has anything to do with the Fourth Amendment. Just as an example, you know, your Fitbit or Apple watch might measure heartbeat and that information might be transmitted into the cloud, I still think that's yours even though it's generated by your autonomic nervous system as opposed to the fact that you've written a journal. It just seems to me that if you have control over the data, you can turn it on, you can turn it off, you can delete it, it just doesn't matter if it's created by taking a photo as opposed to by the fact that you've decided to go somewhere. Similarly from a privacy perspective, I don't see why a photo you take outside is somehow more private than where you were that day because you don't have an expectation of privacy in, like, the thing that you were seeing if you were outside but you do have an expectation of privacy in all of your photos. And likewise, you have an expectation of privacy in everywhere you've gone. So I think that if the Court accepts the government's concession, that you have an expectation of privacy or a property interest in photos and e-mails, the same thing would be the case for location history. As to the warrant on the step 1 issue, Justice Jackson suggested that what happened here is that the government received a list of like 19 different people that were in the geofence. But respectfully, I don't think that's what happened. What it actually got is all of the movements of those 19 people within that hour stretch. So it's a little bit like going into 19 apartments and taking a complete inventory of everything in the apartment but not disclosing the person's name because if you look at the record, like all of those granular movements for that entire hour were exposed. And so that's why I think that the Ybarra case is directly on point here. You don't have probably cause to search based on somebody's proximity to the crime. What happened here is each person's, what we regard as a virtual storage locker, was searched solely because of their proximity to the crime and because of the -- their movements within the hour were exposed every two minutes. That's different from simply identifying which accounts were within the geofence. It's really exposure of information about them. And although it's nominally anonymous, the record shows it's actually quite easy a lot of the time to figure out exactly who a person is based on a relatively small record of their movements. But, look, I've heard some questions from the bench today about steps 2 and 3. There's clearly a constitutional problem with those steps. I mean, as Justice Jackson suggested, the warrant wasn't particularized. There's no criteria given for identifying those people. In terms of how to decide this case, I think it would be very significant case giving a lot of guidance to the bar if the Court says when a search happened, and, number two, at step 2 and step 3, at a minimum, there was a problem with the warrant, without reaching some of the broader questions about general warrants or particularization if the Court is inclined to resolve the warrant question narrowly because the government has a lot of very striking arguments on the warrant issue that could have significant implications. One is that Google wasn't acting as the government's agent, so it makes a difference that, you know, Google pushed the button as opposed to the police. Another argument that's made is that the fact that software is conducting the search is constitutionally relevant, which could have revolutionary implications when, like, AI is monitoring everything we do as opposed to a human being. Also the arguments that as long as something is nominally anonymous, that makes a Fourth Amendment difference, which also can have radical implications when de-anonymizing someone is very easy. So, like, all of these arguments that the government is using to defend the earlier searches could have very broad implications. So if the Court believes that the warrant is unconstitutional at step 2 and step 3, it has the option of just setting aside those broader questions and deciding the warrant issue narrowly and also deciding that's a search. That would be more than a broad enough opinion to be useful to the bar. And I guess on the final question of whether the Court should decide the question presented, look, it's very hard to see how the Court could decide a question like this outside the context of a motion to suppress. If the Court says the good faith exception applies here, it will apply in every single case. And Justice Alito posed the question of what about all the other people, the 500 million people who were searched? Well, number one, they're not told. All of these warrants are sealed. The reason the outcry doesn't exist is that no one knows that thousands of times per year their accounts are being searched. Second, a 1983 claim by any of those people against the detectives would clearly fail on a qualified immunity basis. So, really, the only way these issues would be litigated is through a motion to suppress in a case exactly like this one. And this is a good vehicle to decide the case because there's an extensive evidentiary record. There is declarations from Google. There's live testimony from Google. You'll never have a case with a more detailed account of the technical aspects of the case than this one. And so that's why I think the Court should decide the Fourth Amendment question in this case.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. The case is submitted.
